newsitem.title: USA: GTE executive killed in Guatemelan air crash.
newsitem.headline: GTE executive killed in Guatemelan air crash.

text.p: GTE Corp.'s vice president of international operations, which account for roughly a quarter of the phone operator's total business, was killed Wednesday in an air crash in Guatemela, Guatemalan aviation officials said.

Bruce Haddad, senior vice president of international operations, and his wife, Dorothy Haddad, were among five people who died early Wednesday when their corporate jet crashed south of Guatemala City, the officials said.
The Stamford, Conn.-based company had no immediate comment on the report of Haddad's death and no official statement on how his death would immediately affect its plans.
GTE Chairman Charles Lee said Wednesday he expected a third of GTE's growth would come from international operations.

The company, which now ranks as the world's eighth largest telecommunication services providers, serves 19.1 million residential and business customers in the United States and more than 6 million customers overseas.
"We expect international to be a source of one-third of earnings growth in the years ahead," Lee said.
The company began its international push more than 20 years ago, well ahead of many other U.S. phone operators, which in recent years have embarked on ambitious overseas expansion plans of their own.
GTE's overseas operations are concentrated primarily in Asia and Latin America and to a lesser extent in Europe.
Many of its overseas efforts have focused on providing wireless communications in countries where a conventional telephone line network does not exist.

GTE has interests in Venezuela, Argentina, the Dominican Republic and is the largest foreign investor in the Canadian telecommunications industry. It is gearing up to launch a nationwide paging service in China.

The Haddads were flying in a corporate jet chartered from a Venezuelan company, which slammed into a mountainside around 3:30 a.m. (4:30 a.m. EST), Guatemala's director of civil aviation, Ronald Peter Zineri, said in an interview.

"I called Peru (where the Haddads were picked up) to confirm the list of passengers, who were Bruce Haddad and Mrs. Dorothy Haddad," Zineri said. Three Venezuelan crew members also were killed, he added.

The plane had taken off from Caracas, Venezuela, picked up the Haddads in Lima, Peru, and was to make a stop in Guatemala City, Guatemala's capital, on its way to Dallas, officials said. "The airplane is completely destroyed and there are no
survivors," said Rony Paz, civil aviation chief of operations.
